title: MA9-06386
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX (also know as XXXX XXXXXX), is an Indian citizen who alleges to be a "Convention refugee" and a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of Section 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The claimant alleged that his problems started on XXXXX 2009, when the police raided his house in connection with his friend XXXXX XXXX, whom he had helped to join the XXXX club of which he was a member.
The claimant was arrested and taken to the police station where he was told that his friend was actually named XXXXX XXXX and that he had helped the terrorists in the recent Mumbai bombing.
The police did not believe that the claimant did not know his friend's whereabouts and tortured him in order to get the information.
The claimant was released after three days, with the help of his father and others.

The municipal counsellor of his town told him that he might not be able to help him the next time, so the claimant was to be sent to relatives in XXXXX XXXX. However, they refused to provide him shelter, so he did not go.
On XXXXX 2009, the police again called him to the police station and questioned him about a visit he had made to the court complex in an effort to get help (unsuccessfully).
He was released the same evening, after being beaten.

The claimant spoke the same day to the head of a XXXXXX, called the XXXXXXX, who included him in a planned XXXX tournament in XXXXX. All of the arrangements for him, including a visa, were made on that day.
The claimant arrived in Toronto on XXXXX 2009. He did not go to the tournament, but came to Montreal and asked for refugee status on 4 April 2009.
I have determined that the claimant, XXXX XXXX, is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection". My reasons follow.
The claimant satisfied me as to his identity by way of his Indian passport.

I had some credibility concerns in this claim. For example, I did not find it plausible that the claimant could have gone to the XXXX XXXX, get confirmation of being included in the team, and having a visa obtained all on the same evening that he was released from the police station.
However, the determinative issue in this case is the availability of an internal flight alternative.
The city of Bangalore was suggested as an internal flight alternative for the claimant.
Response to Information Request, dated 18 January 20061, refers to a variety of sources concerning the issue of Sikh relocation within India.
It indicates that the Indian Constitution allows for freedom of movement and that it was generally respected in practice.

This Response refers to a letter from ENSAAF dated 24 January 2005, that stated that Sikh survivors of human rights abuses could not live safely or securely in any part of India. That letter was based, however, mainly on incidents that occurred in the 1990's, according to the Response.

It also, by contrast, refers to a UK Immigration and Nationality Directorate report from 2005, which stated: "Where the fear is of local police and the individual is not of interest to the central authorities, internal relocation is feasible.

A more recent document, the UK Home Office Country Information Report: India, dated 4 January 20102, states that there were no more checks on newcomers, and that the police did not have the resources to check on newcomers and that there was no system of registration of citizens.

This report refers to the Danish Immigration Services which stated that it believed that a high-profile person would not be able to move elsewhere in India without being traced, but that this would be possible for low-profile people".

Also, a document from the UK Home Office, dated 17 April 20083 , stated that while the Punjab police may be serious about pursuing Sikhs anywhere in India whom they view as hard-core militants, in practice only a handful of militants are would be likely to be targeted for such long-arm law enforcement.
On a balance of probabilities, I conclude, based on the more recent documents, that low-profile persons who are of interest only to the local authorities, could safely relocate elsewhere in India.

According to the claimant's story, the police wanted the claimant to get information about XXXXX because of his friendship with him. This friendship was not, on the evidence a close one. The claimant stated that he would just meet XXXXX at the XXXX club, and they might go to the club canteen and have tea together. He did not do anything else with him and did not go to his family.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that this link to XXXXX is too tenuous for the police to consider the claimant to be either a high-profile person or a hard-core militant. Although the claimant stated that the police come to his house "sometimes" and ask about him, the evidence does not indicate that they considered the claimant himself to be a militant. Also, they were harassing him because he went to the court complex and told them about his police problems.
I find that the claimant's fear is of the local police, and he would not be of sufficient interest to them for them to seek him all over India, even if they would be capable of doing that.

The claimant also does not have the profile of someone who would come to the attention of the authorities if he moved elsewhere in India. I find the evidence analyzed above is not clear on whether the police check up on newcomers by way of tenant verification or otherwise. However, even if the police in Bangalore would do that, I find that this would not cause any risk to the claimant. There is no evidence that the central authorities are interested in him.
As stated above, the claimant is not, on the evidence, suspected of being a hard-core militant. He did not allege that there was a warrant of arrest out for him.

Moreover, the claimant had no trouble leaving the airport in India with his genuine passport. According to a Response to Information Request dated 14 April 20094, the data of passengers leaving on international flights is matched with a suspected criminal data bank.

All of this, coupled with the fact that I have already found that the police in the claimant's village did not consider the claimant himself be a militant, leads me to conclude, on a balance of probabilities, that he is not on any wanted list.
I conclude, therefore, that the claimant could live safely in Bangalore.

I also find that it would be reasonable to expect the claimant to relocate. As a Sikh, the claimant is free to practise his religion anywhere in India, and there are many Sikh communities in the country, including the city above-mentioned5.

He may suffer some hardship in relocating and in finding a job, but there was no evidence produced regarding his particular circumstances, that there would be hardship in relocating that would rise to the level of endangering his life or safety. He is a young man (29 years old) and evidently healthy, since he practises XXXX. As stated by Mr. Justice Letourneau in the Ranganathan case6, there is a high threshold for the unreasonableness test. It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant and actual and concrete evidence of such a condition. That is not the case here.
I find, therefore, that the claimant has an available internal flight alternative elsewhere in India, such as the city of Bangalore.

I determine that the claimant, XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXXX) is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection".
